title.en: Cases: why Russian nouns change their endings

card: Russian shows *who did what to whom* with **endings** instead of word order. A noun has six cases, and each one answers its own question: **кто? что?** (nominative), **кого́? чего́?** (genitive), **кому́? чему́?** (dative), **кого́? что?** (accusative), **кем? чем?** (instrumental), **о ком? о чём?** (prepositional).

sections.body:
English relies on word order: *the dog bites the man* and *the man bites the dog* mean different things only because the words swapped places. Russian marks the roles on the words themselves, so the order is free to do other jobs, such as putting the new or important information last.

**Соба́ка куса́ет челове́ка.** and **Челове́ка куса́ет соба́ка.** both mean *the dog bites the man*: the ending **-а** on **челове́ка** says "this is the one being bitten", wherever it stands. Swap the endings, not the words, to swap the roles: **Челове́к куса́ет соба́ку.**

That is the whole idea of cases: an ending is a small label that tells you the word's job in the sentence.

English still has a little of this: *he / him / his*, *who / whom / whose*. You would never say *him sees I*, because *he* and *him* carry the role. Russian simply does this with every noun, adjective and pronoun.

English also uses prepositions where Russian uses a case alone: *a glass **of** water* is **стака́н воды́** (genitive), *write **with** a pen* is **писа́ть ру́чкой** (instrumental), *give it **to** Anna* is **дать А́нне** (dative).

sections.title: What actually decides the case
sections.body:
Three things choose a case, and once you look for them the choice stops being mysterious:

- **The role in the sentence.** The subject is nominative; the thing directly acted on is accusative.
- **A preposition.** Every preposition takes a fixed case (or two, with a change of meaning): **без** always takes the genitive, **с** meaning *with* always takes the instrumental.
- **A governing word.** Some verbs, adjectives and quantity words demand a case: **помога́ть** + dative, **занима́ться** + instrumental, **мно́го** + genitive.

So when you meet a new verb or preposition, learn it with its case, the way English speakers learn *depend on*.

sections.body: Learn the six questions as a chant, in the traditional order: **кто, кого́, кому́, кого́, кем, о ком**. When you are unsure of a case, ask the question the sentence implies. *I'm thinking about…* о ко́м? → prepositional.

mistakes.why: The dictionary form is the subject form. As a direct object the word must change: **кни́гу**.
English *my brother's book* becomes *the book of my brother*: the owner goes in the genitive, after the thing owned.
